note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII English (Core) board exam 2026, Q.P. code 1/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Answers are model answers and value points written for this portal, not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the following passage carefully :
(1) Jonathan Seagull discovered that boredom, fear and anger are the reasons a gull's life is so short and with those gone from his thought, he lived a long, fine life indeed.
(2) They laughed at him. The other gulls scorned him. 'Such nonsense', they would squawk, as he practised flying, not for food but for the joy of flight itself. But Jonathan, undeterred, flew higher and faster than any gull before him. He learned that the secret to flight was not merely flapping wings, but in knowing the purpose of flying.
(3) 'Break the chain of your thought', he told himself, 'And you break the chains of your body.' In solitude, he mastered loops, dives and rolls. He flew at speeds that blurred the ocean below. The flock cast him out for defying tradition, he discovered that exile was not the end but a beginning. Alone, he found peace. Alone, he found the sky.
(4) One morning, soaring silently above the clouds, Jonathan was joined by two radiant gulls. Their wings shone with light and their presence was calm and sure. 'We've been watching you', they said. 'You're ready to come with us.' 'Where?' Jonathan asked blinking in the sunlight. 'To a higher level of being,' they answered. 'You have learned much but there is more – more to flying, more to being a gull.'
(5) He followed them into a realm where flight was pure thought and time had no meaning. There, gulls didn't fight over scraps of bread or squawk at one another in fear. They flew to understand themselves to explore the limitless. There Jonathan met Chiang, the wisest gull, who told him : 'The only true law is that which leads to freedom – there is no other.'
(6) Jonathan began to teach others what he had learned, sharing not just flight techniques but freedom of thought. 'You can go as far as you wish,' he would say. 'Because you have the right to learn. You have the right to be free.' No longer bound by rules, written in sand, Jonathan soared not just through the skies but through understanding. And as he flew, he knew that greatness is not measured in a wingspan but in the courage to break free.
(Adapted in the CBSE paper from Jonathan Livingston Seagull by Richard Bach.)

(i) According to Jonathan, what was the secret of living a long life? (para 1) (1)
(ii) How did Jonathan's unconventional passion for flying lead to his exclusion from the flock? (para 2) (2)
(iii) 'Break the chains of your thought and you break the chains of your body' suggests : (A) freedom is achieved through physical strength (B) mental liberation is the key to true freedom. (1)
(iv) Complete with ONE advantage (para 3) : It was ironical that Jonathan Seagull's exile did not mean isolation but ______. (1)
(v) What do the two radiant gulls who approached Jonathan most likely represent? (A) rivals sent to watch his skills (B) a hallucination formed out of his loneliness (C) fellow gulls returning from his original flock (D) spiritual guides leading him to a higher plane (1)
(vi) Provide one textual evidence from paragraph 4 to prove 'You are ready to come with us.' (1)
(vii) In Chiang's statement, 'the only true law is that which leads to freedom – there is no other', what does 'the only true law' refer to? (1)
(viii) Select the option that best explains Jonathan's transformation after meeting Chiang : (A) becomes more aggressive and fearless (B) forgets the past and returns to his flock (C) learns to use his skills to dominate the other gulls (D) internalises freedom and shares his wisdom with others (1)
(ix) Complete the analogy with ONE word from paragraph 6 — free : bound :: dropped : ______. (A) soared (B) learned (C) measured (D) break (1)
(x) In what way did Jonathan's journey challenge traditional beliefs? Give an example. (2)
questions.solution: (i) Getting rid of boredom, fear and anger from his thoughts. (ii) He practised flying for the joy and purpose of flight, not for food, which the flock saw as nonsense and defiance of tradition; they scorned him and finally cast him out. (iii) (B). (iv) peace and freedom to master flight (a new beginning). (v) (D). (vi) 'We've been watching you' (or: 'You have learned much but there is more'). (vii) the principle of seeking freedom — of thought and self-discovery — as the highest law above all imposed rules. (viii) (D). (ix) (A) soared. (x) Gulls traditionally flew only to get food and obeyed the flock's rules; Jonathan flew for the joy and purpose of flight, mastered loops, dives and rolls, and later taught others freedom of thought, showing that one's limits are self-imposed.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the following passage carefully :
(1) Introduction : India faces a serious road safety challenge. According to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, over 4.8 lakh road accidents were reported in 2023, leading to 1.72 lakh deaths. Many of these could have been avoided by simple precautions – wearing helmets, fastening seatbelts and following speed limits. These statistics aren't just numbers; they represent lives lost and family dynamics changed forever.
Causes of road accidents in India (2023): overspeeding 56%, drunk driving 8%, no seatbelt/helmet 15%, distraction (mobiles) 6%, mechanical failure 4%, weather/road condition 6%, others 5%.
(2) Methodology : Recognising this, several cities are becoming proactive, especially near school zones. The municipal corporations and traffic police have introduced stricter school-zone safety measures – speed bumps, zebra crossings and digital signboards. This led to a 30% drop in minor accidents near schools, within a year. The success lay in combining infrastructure with awareness. Parents, teachers and traffic marshals helped monitor traffic during school hours.
(3) Survey : It's not just governments stepping up. In many cities, class XI and XII students launched a campaign called 'Ride Right', promoting helmet use among two-wheeler riders. They handed out stickers, ran roadshows and launched a 'No Helmet, No Selfie' challenge that went viral. Over 2000 riders pledged to wear helmets daily. Their success even led to invitations from the municipal body to speak in other schools – proof of how youth-led efforts can spark policy engagement.
(4) Results : Technology is also playing a significant role. Automation through AI-powered traffic cameras, digital signs and automated lights is being implemented in metros to reduce human error and improve monitoring, including pilot projects such as iRASTE and an AI-based road safety pilot to predict and prevent accidents using real-time data and alerts for drivers. These systems have led to a 40% rise in fine collection, showing improved rule enforcement. GPS-based alert systems in school buses now notify parents of speeding or unscheduled stops – another step towards safer school commutes.
(5) Implication for interventions : Still, personal responsibility is the most powerful safety tool. Whether it's a student cyclist using the left lane or a pedestrian waiting for the signal, every right choice sets an example. A popular slogan in school says it best : 'I follow, I influence.' Road safety is about respecting life, valuing time, and leading by example.

(i) What strategy does the author use in paragraph (1) to highlight the seriousness of road accidents? (A) use of statistics and emotional appeal (B) humour and satire (C) technical jargon and neutrality (D) personal anecdotes and optimism (1)
(ii) What evidence suggests that stricter school-zone measures were effective? (A) the number of schools increased rapidly (B) there was a 30% drop in minor accidents near schools (C) teachers and parents opposed the new rules (D) students stopped commuting by bicycle (1)
(iii) What would 'Students launched a campaign called "Ride Right" promoting helmet use among two-wheeler riders' be classified as? (A) primary purpose (B) secondary objective (C) method of analysis (D) research outcome (1)
(iv) Give two points to support the success of the No Helmet – No Selfie challenge. (2)
(v) Which word from paragraph 4 best conveys 'ensuring compliance through authoritative measures' in the context of traffic systems? (A) collection (B) enforcement (C) monitoring (D) automation (1)
(vi) Analyse why the author emphasises that both technology and personal responsibility are important in promoting road safety. (2)
(vii) Complete with a suitable reason : Road safety is about personal responsibility because ______. (1)
(viii) Which inference is best supported by the data in the table? (A) enforcement of helmet and seat belt rules would address the cause of road deaths (B) speeding is the key issue, which requires technological and behavioural interventions (C) mobile phone use while driving is the fastest growing cause of accidents (D) drunk driving accounts for more deaths than 'no helmet/seat belt' and distractions combined (1)
questions.solution: (i) (A). (ii) (B). (iii) (C) method of analysis (portal's reading; it describes how the survey data on the youth campaign was gathered). (iv) It went viral; over 2000 riders pledged to wear helmets daily; the students were invited by the municipal body to speak in other schools. (v) (B) enforcement. (vi) Technology (AI cameras, automated lights, GPS alerts) reduces human error and improves monitoring and enforcement, but it cannot make every choice for road users; each person's disciplined behaviour (wearing helmets, obeying signals) prevents accidents and sets an example, so both are needed together. (vii) every individual's right choice on the road saves lives and influences others to follow ('I follow, I influence'). (viii) (B) — overspeeding causes 56% of accidents.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: Your school is organising a career counselling session for students of classes XI and XII to help them make informed decisions about their future career choices. As the Head Girl / Head Boy of M.L.C. School, draft a notice in about 50 words informing them about the session. Include all necessary details. You are Riya / Rohan. Put the notice in a box.
questions.solution: Format (1): school name, NOTICE, date, heading, name and designation. Content (2): purpose, date, time, venue, resource persons/counsellors, eligible classes, registration details. Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: You are Kavya / Karan, Chief Editor of 'Parakh', the school magazine. Draft a notice in about 50 words inviting contributions in the form of articles, stories, poems, artwork etc. for the special annual edition. All contributions are to be submitted to the Chief Editor. Include necessary details. Put your notice in a box.
questions.solution: Format (1): school name, NOTICE, date, heading, signature. Content (2): types of contributions, theme (if any), word limit, last date, where and to whom to submit, original work only. Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: Draft an invitation in about 50 words to invite the M.L.A. of your constituency to be the Chief Guest at a felicitation function to honour eminent residents who have contributed to the upliftment of the colony. Mention one compelling highlight of the programme. You are Satupa / Satish, President of the Surya Vikas RWA.
questions.solution: Format (1): formal letter/invitation layout with address, date, salutation, close. Content (2): occasion, request to be chief guest, date, time, venue, one highlight (e.g. a cultural programme by children or release of a colony souvenir), confirmation request. Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: You are Dr. Vora, a certified art therapist from Manipur. You have been invited by Green Valley Public School, Jammu to conduct a seminar on 'Art Therapy, the Way Forward' for the students. Draft a reply in about 50 words accepting the invitation.
questions.solution: Format (1). Content (2): thanks, acceptance, confirmation of date, time, topic, and requirements (art materials, projector, audience size). Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: You are Kaneshta / Shirish, an avid yoga follower. Write a letter to the editor in 120-150 words expressing your views and urging people, especially students and young adults, to incorporate yoga into their daily lives. (Cues: need to follow a disciplined exercise routine; reduces stress, improves physical and mental health; increases focus; schools and educational establishments must encourage the practice of yoga.)
questions.solution: Format (1): sender's address, date, The Editor, subject, salutation, close. Content (3): sedentary lifestyles and stress among youth; benefits of yoga for body and mind, focus and discipline; suggestions for schools and colleges (daily sessions, trained instructors, Yoga Day). Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: You are Roshni / Rohan, a final year student pursuing a degree in Computer Science. You have read an advertisement in 'The National Times' by Tech Innovate Solutions for AI Engineers (qualifications: bachelor's degree in Computer Science/IT; skills: proficiency with AI frameworks, understanding of data science, familiarity with PyTorch and Python; experience: 1–2 years' work experience, projects, certifications; write to the Public Relations Officer, Tech Innovate Solutions, Markhande Lane, Pune). Write a job application along with your bio-data in 120-150 words.
questions.solution: Format (1): letter plus separate bio-data. Content (3): reference to the advertisement, interest and suitability; bio-data with qualifications (B.Tech/B.Sc. Computer Science, final year), skills (Python, PyTorch, AI frameworks, data science), internships/projects, certifications, references. Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: You are Aanya / Ankit. You are deeply disturbed by how moments of silence and relaxed living are vanishing from today's fast-paced lives. Write an article in 120-150 words for the newspaper on 'The Vanishing Art of Slowing Down'. (Cues: impact of hustle culture and technology on mental well-being; losing connection with nature, people and self; importance of mindful celebrations and slow, relaxed living; role of schools, communities and media; need for digital boundaries, reflection and simple joys.)
questions.solution: Format (1): title and byline. Content (3): the problem of constant rush and screens; effects on mental health and relationships; value of slowing down — mindfulness, nature, family time; what schools, communities and media can do; practical suggestions such as digital detox and hobbies. Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: Your school organised a 'Tastes of India' Week to educate students on the diversity of Indian cuisine. Write a comprehensive report in 120-150 words detailing the activities conducted during the week — the events, participation, chief guest and overall impact on the school. You are Arti / Aryan, a student of Std. XII and Secretary of the School Magazine Editorial Board. (Organise by What – When – Where – Who – Why – How.)
questions.solution: Format (1): heading, byline, place and date. Content (3): dates and venue, inauguration and chief guest, regional food stalls, cooking demonstrations, quiz and talks on nutrition, student participation, impact (appreciation of cultural diversity and healthy eating). Expression (1).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
It would be an exotic moment
without rush, without engines.
we would all be together
in sudden strangeness
Fishermen in the cold sea
would not harm whales
and the man gathering salt
would look at his hurt hands. (Keeping Quiet)

(i) What does the phrase 'an exotic moment' signify? (A) surreal pause from mechanised human activity enabling reflection and unity (B) ceremonial halt wherein humans acknowledge traditional and ecological wisdom (C) spontaneous event where all human labour becomes obsolete (D) rare disruption of routine that highlights cultural diversity and isolation
(ii) Complete : The words 'we' and 'together' signify ______.
(iii) The excerpt tells us that the poet ______ (condemns / glorifies) the moment 'without rush, without engines'.
(iv) Choose the option that BEST reflects the tone of the poet : (A) despairing and cynical (B) aggressive and accusatory (C) meditative and hopeful (D) humorous and sarcastic
(v) Complete : The phrase 'hurt hands' is a symbol of ______.
(vi) What message is the poet conveying through the extract?
questions.solution: (i) (A). (ii) unity and universal brotherhood — all people sharing the moment of silence. (iii) glorifies. (iv) (C). (v) the suffering and exploitation of labourers (the toll of hard, relentless work). (vi) A moment of collective silence and introspection would stop harm to nature and to ourselves and bring peace and unity.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
You have the money, but if you want to be mean
Why keep your money (this crossly) and go along
The hurt to the scenery, wouldn't be my complaint
So much as the trusting sorrow of what is unsaid :
Here far from the city we make our roadside stand
And ask for some city money to feel in hand
To try if it will not make our being expand,
And give us the life of the moving-pictures' promise
That the party in power is said to be keeping from us. (A Roadside Stand)

(i) What emotion does the speaker reveal when he says 'if you want to be mean, why keep your money (this crossly) and go along'? (A) curiosity (B) bitterness (C) indifference (D) detachment
(ii) What does the speaker imply in 'The hurt to the scenery wouldn't be my complaint'?
(iii) Complete : The word 'expand' in 'to try if it will not make our being expand' implies an aspiration to ______.
(iv) Assertion (A): The speaker critiques the governing party for withholding opportunities from the rural poor. Reason (R): The extract praises the government for their promises of a life of the moving pictures. (A) Both true, R explains A (B) Both true, R does not explain A (C) A true, R false (D) A false, R true
(v) Which concern is NOT explored in the extract? (A) political manipulation of rural dreams (B) discrimination faced due to different religious policies (C) transactional disconnection between the city and the village (D) impact of unfulfilled expectations
(vi) State in one sentence what advice an address to politicians drawn from this extract is most likely to include.
questions.solution: (i) (B). (ii) He is not really bothered that the stand spoils the view; what hurts him is the silent, trusting sorrow of the poor who wait in vain for customers. (iii) lead a better, more prosperous life (grow economically and as human beings). (iv) (C). (v) (B). (vi) Politicians should keep their promises and genuinely work to improve the lives of the rural poor instead of making empty promises.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
I cried aloud, shaking my head all the while until I felt the cold blades of the scissors against my neck, and heard them gnaw off one of my thick braids. Then I lost my spirit. Since the day I was taken from my mother, I had suffered extreme indignities. People had stared at me. I had been tossed about in the air like a wooden puppet. And now my long hair was shingled like a coward's! In my anguish, I moaned for my mother, but no one came to comfort me. Not a soul reasoned quietly with me, as my own mother used to do; for now I was only one of many little animals driven by a herder. (Memories of Childhood)

(i) Complete : 'Then I lost my spirit' indicates that the speaker ______.
(ii) What does Zitkala-Sa imply about the prejudice prevailing in society when she talks of having 'suffered extreme indignities'?
(iii) Why did Zitkala-Sa yearn to be with her mother in her moment of anguish?
(iv) The tone of the narrator can be best described as (A) bitter and strong willed (B) detached and impersonal (C) pained and despairing (D) grateful and reflective
questions.solution: (i) gave up resisting and felt helpless and defeated. (ii) The European school authorities treated Native American children with contempt, disregarding their culture and dignity. (iii) Her mother used to comfort her and reason with her gently, while at school no one understood or consoled her. (iv) (C).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.chapter: Vistas: On the Face of It
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
Derry : But I'm not.... I'm not afraid [pause] people are afraid of me.
Mr. Lamb : Why should that be?
Derry : Everyone is. It doesn't matter who they are, or what they say, or how they look. How they pretend. I know. I can see.
Mr. Lamb : See what?
Derry : What they think?
Mr. Lamb : What do they think, then?
Derry : You think.... 'Here's a boy'. You look at me... and then you see my face and you think. That's bad. That's a terrible thing. 'That's the ugliest thing I ever saw.' You think, 'poor boy'. But I'm not. Not poor. Underneath, you are afraid. Anybody would be – I am. When I look in the mirror, and see it, I'm afraid of me.
Mr. Lamb : No, not the whole of you. Not of you.
Derry : Yes! (On the Face of It)

(i) Which emotion dominates Derry's dialogue? (A) superiority (B) shrewdness (C) vulnerability (D) indifference
(ii) Complete : According to Derry, people put up a pretence when they see him because ______.
(iii) When Mr. Lamb says, 'No, not the whole of you. Not of you,' he means : (A) your face will get healed and your ideas about your appearance will change (B) you are not just your face or your injury; that is not the sum total of who you are (C) I am afraid of your face and your appearance (D) you shouldn't look into the mirror so that you don't get the feeling of dejection
(iv) State in one sentence what advice you would give to the people who pretend to look away when they see Derry's face.
questions.solution: (i) (C). (ii) they are actually frightened or repelled by his burnt face but try to hide it out of politeness. (iii) (B). (iv) Treat him normally and with respect, looking at the person rather than the scar, without pity or fear.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
The make-up room had the look of a hair-cutting salon with lights at all angles around half a dozen large mirrors. They were all incandescent lights, so you can imagine the fiery misery of those subjected to make-up. The make-up department was first headed by a Bengali who became too big for the studio and left. He was succeeded by a Maharashtrian who was assisted by a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and the usual local Tamils. All this shows that there was a great deal of National Integration long before A.I.R. and Doordarshan began broadcasting programmes on national integration. This gang of nationally integrated make-up men could turn any decent-looking person into a hideous crimson hued monster with the help of truckloads of pancake and a number of other locally made potions and lotions. Those were the days of mainly indoor shooting, and only five percent of the film was shot outdoors. I suppose the sets and studio lights needed girls and boys to be made to look ugly in order to look presentable in the movie. A strict hierarchy was maintained in the make-up department. (Poets and Pancakes)

(i) Why did the make-up room have the look of a hair-cutting salon?
(ii) What does 'fiery misery of those subjected to make-up' suggest? (A) emotional stress faced by the actors (B) physical discomfort due to heat and lighting (C) anger of the make-up artists due to irritation (D) the discomfort caused by the cramped room
(iii) Complete : The tone of the author in the phrase 'hideous crimson hued monster' is ______.
(iv) Why was excessive make-up considered a cinematic necessity at Gemini Studios during that era? (A) minimised the cost of set design and costumes (B) was a mandated practice by the studio's creative heads and lead actors (C) aligned with the theatrical traditions the studio admired (D) compensated for the lack of advanced lighting and camera technology
(v) What does 'became too big for the studio and left' imply about the Bengali make-up artist?
(vi) Complete with a suitable reason : The author refers to the presence of people from different regions in the make-up department to ______.
questions.solution: (i) It had lights at all angles around half a dozen large mirrors. (ii) (B). (iii) humorous / satirical (gently mocking). (iv) (D) — with mostly indoor shooting under harsh studio lights, heavy make-up was needed to look presentable on screen. (v) He became so successful and famous (or proud) that the studio could no longer hold him, so he left for better opportunities. (vi) humorously show that national integration existed in the studio long before A.I.R. and Doordarshan promoted it.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the questions :
'Now I am going to tell you, Mr. Ironmaster, how things are', he said. 'The whole world is nothing but a big rattrap. All the good things that are offered to you are nothing but cheese rinds and bits of pork, set out to drag a poor fellow into trouble. And if the sheriff comes now and locks me up for this, then you, Mr. Ironmaster, must remember that a day will come when you yourself may want to get a big piece of pork, and then you will get caught in the trap.'
The ironmaster began to laugh.
'That was not so badly said, my good fellow. Perhaps we should let the sheriff alone on Christmas Eve.' (The Rattrap)

(i) What does the speaker mean by 'The whole world is nothing but a big rattrap'? (A) The world offers many chances for success and prosperity (B) Temptations in life are traps that lead people into trouble (C) Good deeds are always rewarded with cheese rinds (D) Justice and fairness are not guaranteed for everyone
(ii) What does the phrase 'cheese rinds' showcase? (A) temptation (B) affirmation (C) gluttony (D) deprivation
(iii) By calling himself a 'poor fellow', the speaker emphasises his ______. (vulnerability / credibility)
(iv) What does the speaker imply through his warning to the ironmaster?
(v) What does 'Perhaps we should let the sheriff alone on Christmas Eve' showcase about the ironmaster's nature? (A) materialistic (B) understanding (C) conniving (D) enterprising
(vi) Complete with a suitable reason : It is implied that the speaker would be locked up because ______.
questions.solution: (i) (B). (ii) (A). (iii) vulnerability. (iv) Even a rich man like the ironmaster can be lured by greed for bigger gains and fall into the trap of worldly temptations. (v) (B) (good-humoured and lenient). (vi) he had accepted the invitation under a false identity, letting the ironmaster believe he was his old comrade (and was a vagabond, possibly a thief).

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: The poem explores the relationship between a mother and daughter. Comment. (40-50 words)
questions.solution: The poet loves her mother deeply; seeing her ageing, pale face on the drive to the airport, she feels the old childhood fear of losing her. She hides her pain behind a smile and says 'see you soon, Amma', showing tender love and the helplessness of separation.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: What does Umberto Eco mean when he says he is 'a professor who writes novels on Sundays'? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: He sees himself mainly as an academic scholar whose identity rests on teaching and philosophy; novel writing is a pastime he enjoys in his spare time, done in the 'interstices', not his primary profession.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: The British landlords agreed to refund 25% of the money to the sharecroppers in the Champaran dispute. What is the significance of this event? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: The amount mattered less than the principle: the landlords had to surrender part of the money and their prestige, which taught the peasants that they had rights and could stand up fearlessly, an important step towards self-reliance and freedom.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: How did Douglas' experience at the beach in California affect him? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: At three or four years of age, waves knocked him down and buried him at a beach in California; this left him terrified of water, an aversion that grew into a lasting fear.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: The constraints of Aunt Jennifer's married life leave her terrorised and emotionally scarred. Elaborate. (40-50 words)
questions.solution: Her fingers flutter and struggle to pull the needle because the 'massive weight of Uncle's wedding band' sits heavily on her hand; the oppressive marriage has made her timid, and even in death her hands will remain 'ringed with ordeals'.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: 'Will they make them sing in German, even the pigeons?' What does Franz's remark suggest about the imposition of German in school in Alsace? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: It reveals the absurdity and harshness of the Prussian order forcing German on the Alsatians; a language and culture cannot be imposed by force, any more than pigeons could be made to coo in German.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: What does Bama's decision to excel in academics reveal about her character? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: On her brother's advice that education alone could win respect, she studied hard and stood first; it shows her determination, self-respect and courage to fight caste discrimination through knowledge.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: How did the newspaper 'The World' contribute to Charley's belief in the existence of the third level? (40-50 words)
questions.solution: He collected first-day covers, and among his stamps he found a letter from Sam, postmarked 1894 and addressed to him, saying Sam had found the third level and settled in Galesburg; this convinced Charley it was real.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: Evaluate the role of the court astrologer in shaping the trajectory of the Tiger King's life. (40-50 words)
questions.solution: The astrologer predicted that the king would be killed by a tiger (the hundredth tiger); to defy this, the king killed tigers obsessively, married to get more tigers and ruined his state's wildlife — ultimately dying from a tiger in the form of a wooden toy, fulfilling the prophecy.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: Sophie in 'Going Places' and Mukesh in 'Lost Spring' aspire to a better life, yet external forces shape their realities and opportunities. Discuss. (120-150 words)
questions.solution: Value points: Sophie, from a poor working-class family, dreams of owning a boutique, being an actress or a fashion designer and of meeting the footballer Danny Casey, but her family's poverty and lack of opportunity mean she is destined to work in a biscuit factory; her dreams remain fantasies. Mukesh, from a family of bangle makers in Firozabad, dreams of becoming a motor mechanic despite poverty, caste, a vicious circle of moneylenders, middlemen and police, and tradition. Both have dreams, but social and economic forces limit them; Mukesh's dream is more realistic and shows will to break free, while Sophie escapes into fantasy.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.chapter: Flamingo: My Mother at Sixty-six / A Thing of Beauty
questions.text: How is the transient nature of beauty and life portrayed in the poems 'My Mother at Sixty-six' and 'A Thing of Beauty'? (120-150 words)
questions.solution: Value points: Kamala Das sees her mother's ashen, corpse-like face and realises she is ageing and nearing death; the images of trees sprinting and children spilling out of homes contrast youth with old age, showing life's impermanence and the fear of loss. Keats acknowledges life's sorrow, gloom and 'despondence', but says a thing of beauty is a joy forever, never passing into nothingness; beautiful things (sun, moon, trees, daffodils, tales of the mighty dead) give lasting joy that binds us to the earth despite suffering. One poem dwells on transience, the other finds permanence in beauty that consoles us against it.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.chapter: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.text: Examine how the presence of school students on the expedition contributes to the message of environmental responsibility and hope. (120-150 words)
questions.solution: Value points: Geoff Green's Students on Ice programme takes high-school students to Antarctica, which holds the history of the Earth and shows the impact of climate change clearly (shrinking glaciers, collapsing ice shelves). Young students are future policy makers; seeing the fragile ecosystem first-hand gives them understanding and respect for the planet at an impressionable age. Lessons like the importance of phytoplankton show how small changes affect the whole system. Their awareness and enthusiasm offer hope that the next generation will act responsibly to protect the environment.

questions.subject: English Core
questions.text: How does Pearl S. Buck explore the theme of humanitarianism versus patriotism in the lesson 'The Enemy'? Support your answer with evidence from the text. (120-150 words)
questions.solution: Value points: Dr. Sadao, a loyal Japanese surgeon, finds a wounded American prisoner of war on the beach during the war. As a patriot he should hand him over, but as a doctor he cannot let a man die. He and Hana treat him, risking their lives; the servants leave in protest. He informs the General, who plans to have the man killed but forgets. Sadao then helps the soldier escape by boat, with food and clothing. Buck shows that humanity and compassion rise above narrow patriotism and the hatred of war; Sadao balances both by reporting to the General yet saving the man's life.
